notes:
SESSION-CLOSE CONTEXT DUMP — T212 worker. Five sections: (1) hypotheses ruled out, (2) hazards noticed, (3) deliverable weaknesses, (4) tooling/process friction, (5) inter-progress-line gap analysis per build phase.

=== (1) HYPOTHESES FORMED AND RULED OUT ===

H1: Runner's auto-claim failure was harmless.
  Formed when: first run with --task-id T212 exited after 3 lines of log.
  Ruled out by: reading tools/runner line 540 — sys.exit(1) on claim failure.
  The runner treats ANY non-zero exit from 'managent claim' as fatal, including
  'ALREADY CLAIMED'. Since I had already claimed T212 manually, the runner's
  auto-claim failed and the runner killed the build before it started.
  Resolution: dropped --task-id flag; claimed manually first per DELEGATEE.md.

H2: The artifact SHA-256 not changing meant the fix was a no-op.
  Formed when: shasum -a 256 on the WZO2 file returned a892d689… (same as T192/T193).
  Ruled IN (hypothesis was correct about the file), FALSE about the rebuild.
  The builder prints the artifact summary lines BEFORE writing to disk. The old
  file from T192 was still on disk. The build process was still running (PID alive
  at 3887 MB RSS). After the process exited, the SHA-256 was 0c3366f0… — different.
  Ruled out by: checking liveness with ps, then waiting for completion.

H3: The acceptance stdout was truncated due to zig's print buffering.
  Formed when: stdout capture files were missing A3/A5/A6 summary lines but
  showed the last A9 lines and OVERALL VERDICT.
  Ruled IN by: running through Python subprocess.run with capture_output=True,
  which properly drains pipes. The Threaded IO in util.out() uses
  std.Io.Threaded; the IO thread sometimes doesn't flush before process exit.
  This is a known weakness in util.zig — not my bug, but it cost me time.

H4 (SPECULATION): The passes-bit fix might change the root values.
  Ruled out: root values are identical to T192 (empty B: L=+1 H=+16,
  empty W: L=-16 H=-1). The fix only changes the key_byte encoding, not the
  L/H/DTT values computed by the fixpoint solver. The fixpoint results are
  byte-identical to the pre-fix build — only the sort order and lookup keys differ.

=== (2) HAZARDS OR FRAGILE ASSUMPTIONS NOTICED BUT NOT INVESTIGATED ===

HAZARD-1: DTT phase has zero per-sweep progress output.
  The builder emits '# DTT: iterative relaxation (max 254 sweeps)...' at the
  start of DTT, then NOTHING until '# DTT sweep 10: changed=0' after all 10 sweeps
  complete. A watchdog polling for output would see a ~6-8 minute silence and
  cannot distinguish 'DTT sweep 3 is slow' from 'the process is hung'.
  Mitigation recommendation: add per-sweep output like the fixpoint has, or at
  least a heartbeat every N states processed.

HAZARD-2: Fixpoint convergence is oscillatory, not monotonic.
  L_changed values across sweeps: 24.4M, 2.0M, 9.2M, 18.2M, 25.1M, 28.7M,
  29.5M, 27.0M, 21.6M, 14.9M, 8.7M, 4.2M, 1.7M, 570K, 173K, 48K, 13.8K,
  5.2K, 4.4K, 6.2K, 6.4K, 3.3K, 2.1K, 6.0K, 13.9K, 12.7K, 5.4K, 1.5K,
  252, 16, 0.
  Notice the non-monotonicity: sweep 24 has 6.0K changes, sweep 25 jumps to
  13.9K, sweep 26 stays at 12.7K. Then it drops and converges. A
  'converged-early' heuristic based on changes < N would be fooled at sweep
  15 (173K) or sweep 19 (4.4K) only to see a spike at 25 (13.9K). The current
  convergence condition (exactly zero changes) is the only safe one.

HAZARD-3: Artifact overwrites in place — no atomic rename.
  If the build is SIGKILLed during the write phase, the previous artifact
  (valid or invalid) is destroyed. There is no write-to-temp-then-rename
  pattern. The write of 518 MB over ~30-60 seconds creates a vulnerability
  window. This did not bite me (runner didn't kill during write), but it
  could in future runs. SPECULATION: this is low-priority because the build
  is deterministic and can be re-run, but it's a data-integrity gap.

HAZARD-4: SHA-256 self-check during write verifies in-memory data, not disk data.
  The log shows: '# SHA-256 self-check...' then '# SHA-256 verified' then
  '# Writing untracked/...' then '# WZO2 artifact written: ...'.
  The SHA-256 verification happens BEFORE the file is written to disk. It
  verifies that the header's embedded hash matches the computed hash of the
  in-memory buffer. It does NOT verify that the bytes on disk match. The
  M4a A9 check does a proper read-back verification (reads the file, computes
  hash, compares to embedded hash), and A9 passes. So the end-to-end integrity
  is covered by the acceptance check, but the builder's self-check is weaker
  than the log suggests.

HAZARD-5 (SPECULATION): The 21600s CPU ceiling may be tight for future runs.
  This run used 4064s CPU. If the fixpoint ever needs more sweeps (e.g.,
  different ruleset, different ko handling), the 6-hour ceiling could be
  breached. The runner defaults (3600s CPU) are clearly inadequate for 4×4.
  The 4×4 build should document its expected CPU budget: ~4100s observed.

=== (3) DELIVERABLE WEAKNESSES — THINGS I WOULD NOT DEFEND ===

WEAK-1: I did not verify fixpoint correctness independently.
  M4a acceptance checks format consistency (A3 colour inversion, A5 round-trip,
  A6 calibration, A9 reproducibility). None of these checks verify that the
  fixpoint values are game-theoretically correct. The AGENTS.md forecloses on
  trusting the ko-sensitive values. The M4a PASS means the artifact is
  well-formed and self-consistent; it does not mean the scores are right.
  This is as-designed (M4a is a format check, not a correctness proof) and
  the brief didn't ask for correctness verification, but it's worth stating.

WEAK-2: A5 round-trip is insensitive to the passes-bit bug.
  T193's A5 passed (0 mismatches on stride 97) even with the buggy artifact.
  My A5 also passes. This means A5 is not evidence that the fix worked — it's
  evidence that the fix didn't BREAK the round-trip encoding. A3 and A9 are
  the checks that actually catch the bug. The 1% sampling rate (stride 97)
  is adequate for format validation but would miss a sparse encoding bug.

WEAK-3: The per-sweep fixpoint numbers are reported but not cross-referenced.
  I didn't diff the fixpoint sweep outputs against T192's run. They SHOULD
  be identical (same algorithm, same input, same fix). I assume they are but
  haven't verified. The root values match T192. SPECULATION: the full sweep
  trace is likely identical bit-for-bit.

WEAK-4 (SPECULATION): The embedded SHA-256 in the artifact (57009d93…) is
  the hash of the data sections (L, H, DTT arrays), not of the full file.
  The file-level SHA-256 (0c3366f0…) differs from the old one (a892d689…)
  ONLY because the key_bytes changed. The L/H/DTT values embedded in the new
  artifact should be byte-identical to the old artifact. If someone diffs
  the two artifacts, the only differences should be in the per-entry key_bytes
  for passes=1 entries. I haven't verified this byte-level claim.

=== (4) WHERE THE BRIEF, TOOLING, OR DOCS MISLED ME OR COST TIME ===

COST-1: Runner --task-id + pre-claimed task = silent kill (10 min lost).
  The brief says 'use tools/runner' but doesn't mention the --task-id
  interaction. I claimed T212 manually (per DELEGATEE.md), then ran with
  --task-id T212. The runner tried to auto-claim, got ALREADY CLAIMED, and
  exited 1 before launching zig. The log was 3 lines. I assumed the build
  started but was slow; after 60s I checked ps and found no zig process.
  Fix: either the brief should say 'claim manually, do not use --task-id'
  or the runner should treat ALREADY CLAIMED as success (exit 0, continue).

COST-2: util.out's Threaded IO drops lines on process exit (20 min lost).
  The acceptance instrument uses std.Io.Threaded for stdout. When the process
  exits, the IO thread may not have flushed all buffered writes. Capturing
  stdout via shell redirection (zig run … > file) produced truncated output
  missing A3/A5/A6 summary lines. I re-ran three times before trying Python's
  subprocess, which properly drains. This is a project-level bug in util.zig
  — any agent running oracle_v2_accept.zig via shell redirection will see
  truncated output. Workaround: use Python subprocess, or fix util.out to
  either not use Threaded IO or finalize the IO thread before exit.

COST-3: Runner default CPU ceiling (3600s) is undocumented hazard for 4×4.
  The brief says 'OOM discipline from T192 stands' and T192 used 14400s wall.
  It did NOT mention the CPU ceiling. The runner default of 3600s CPU
  silently killed the first build at the DTT boundary — fixpoint converged,
  DTT started, then SIGKILL. The hour of fixpoint work was wasted. The
  runner docs (docs/infra/runner.md) state the default but the brief didn't
  flag that 4×4 needs more. This is a process gap: 4×4 builder runs should
  document their required ceilings in the brief.

COST-4 (MINOR): The builder re-does the gate chain on every run.
  The gate chain (2×2, 3×2, 3×3) re-runs every time the 4×4 builder is
  invoked. This costs maybe 30s and is harmless but unnecessary — the gate
  chain passes every time. Not a real issue, just noticed.

=== (5) INTER-PROGRESS-LINE GAP ANALYSIS ===

METHODOLOGY NOTE: The builder log has NO timestamps on individual lines.
Only the runner emits wall/CPU totals at exit. Per-phase timing is estimated
from the run-1/run-2 wall delta (run-1 killed at DTT start at 3604.3s;
run-2 completed at 4067.9s; DTT+build+write ≈ 463.6s wall) and from the
structure of the computation. These are ESTIMATES, not measurements.
Speculation is labelled.

Phase breakdown (run-2, 4067.9s wall, 4063.6s CPU):

  Phase                    Lines  Progress?  Est. wall    Longest silence
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Gate chain (2×2,3×2,3×3)   22    per-gate     ~30s        ~10s (SPEC: between gobans)
  Census (4×4 BFS)           51    per-sweep   ~120s        ~15s (SPEC: within frontier sweeps)
  Fixpoint hash build          3    once         ~60s        ~60s (SPEC: insert 99M, no progress)
  Fixpoint sweeps (×31)       58    per-sweep  ~3450s       ~200s (SPEC: early sweep over 99M, 29M changes)
  DTT sweeps (×10)             2    start+end   ~350s       **~350s** (MEASURED: zero per-sweep lines)
  Build artifact (in mem)      9    per-metric   ~10s        ~2s (SPEC)
  Write artifact (to disk)     7    per-stage   ~100s       ~60s (SPEC: 518 MB write)
  Summary                      4    —            ~1s        —

  TOTAL: ~145 lines over ~4068s wall

Key gap (MEASURED, not speculated):
  The DTT phase emits exactly TWO lines during its entire computation:
    Line 1: '# DTT: iterative relaxation (max 254 sweeps)...'
    Line 2: '# DTT sweep 10: changed=0'
  All 10 DTT sweeps (processing 99M states each, simpler per-state computation
  than fixpoint but still 99M iterations) produce ZERO intermediate output.
  The estimated silence duration is ~350s (5.8 min). This is the number a
  watchdog/staleness detector needs to accommodate.

Fixpoint sweep timing (ESTIMATED, not measured):
  Total fixpoint sweeps: 31, ~3450s wall, ~111s per sweep average.
  But sweeps are NOT uniform — the per-sweep work is proportional to the
  number of states whose L or H value changed in the previous sweep.
  Early sweeps (1-12): 2M-29M changes/sweep, likely 100-300s each.
  Late sweeps (20-31): 16-14000 changes/sweep, likely 10-60s each.
  The longest single-sweep silence is likely sweep 7 (29.5M changes) at
  ~200-300s (SPECULATION — without timestamps, this is a guess from the
  change-count distribution).

  For a watchdog: the WORST-CASE gap between fixpoint progress lines is
  probably 200-300s (early sweep). The DTT gap (~350s) is longer.
  If you set a staleness watchdog to 600s (10 min), you cover both.
  The current runner default of 3600s CPU ceiling is fine as a budget
  but not as a staleness detector — it only fires at the end, not on
  silence.

Census gap:
  32 sweeps over ~120s, ~4s per sweep average. Early sweeps process
  larger frontiers (up to 22M) but the per-state work is O(neighbour-count),
  much lighter than fixpoint's minimax. Silence gaps likely <30s.

Write gap (SPECULATION):
  The 518 MB write to disk has no intermediate progress. On this machine
  it took ~60-100s. A 'writing X%' progress emitter would close this gap.

RECOMMENDATION: The DTT phase is the largest silence and the one most
likely to trigger a false-positive watchdog kill. Adding a per-sweep
progress line ('# DTT sweep N: changed=M' like the fixpoint has) would
reduce the max silence from ~350s to ~35s per sweep, making a 120s
watchdog viable.
